title: You Will Migrate Eventually: A developer approach to technology adoption

segments.text: Thank you. Look at with how many you came. I'm really I'm really flattered. And I shouldn't stand here. So, you will migrate eventually. Thank you.
Don't you ever think that when you see a piece of code that's you see in the in your post or you think who who the hell wrote this piece of
code? This is really garbage. And then you look at the git blame and you see, "Oh, yeah, that that was me." At some point, you have to change the
code that you write. But, when we are writing code, we never really think about that. We never really think about the code that we will change, the code
that we have to throw away. We just think about let's just write it. Let's just ship it and let's get it over with. But, you will have to change it one way
or another. If you don't, you will be forced or something will break and it will get stuck. So, software is not fixed. And I think Lehman's Lehman's law
mentioned this perfectly. Lehman's law is about software evolution says that the only constant thing in software evolution is change. Not just about the code, it's about the teams, it's about
the structure, it's about the organization, it's about everything around it. ING is a big company. We have many applications and more than 20,000 engineers.
And that makes sense because when you look at a bank, it's actually software. We go to the website, we go to the app, we do our banking, we do our finances
all through technology. So, we're a big software company. And that also means we have a lot of a lot of migrations and a lot of
changes. ING originally uh was from the Netherlands and we acquired banks in different countries. Now, I just want to see a raise of hands. Who here has a bank account with
ING? Well, that's a that's a lot of hands. Now, another question. Who of you here has an an ING account outside of Germany? That's also still quite a few hands.
Then, the interesting thing is that if you have a bank account outside of ING Germany, you might actually also know us under a different name. In Romania, we
are known as ING Home'Bank. In Poland, we are known as ING Slaski. Well, even in Germany, a lot of people still know us as ING DiBa, even though we don't use
that name anymore. We migrated away from it. Getting these banks and putting them into one also meant migrations. Migrations not just of the brands, like
making it orange, but also of the tech stack. And that comes with quite a lot of challenges. Hello, I'm Wouter Lichtenberg. I'm a director engineering of, uh, of this
bank in inside ING in Germany. In my career, the last 10 years, uh, working for ING, I've worked in the Netherlands, Philippines, Romania, and now I'm
working here in Germany. So, you could say I've also migrated myself a lot, uh, throughout my years. >> Hi everyone, and my name is Luisa Ring,
and for the past around 6 years, I've worked on several change projects in different countries. I worked in the US and in Australia, in Germany, of course,
as well, and I recently moved to the Netherlands for to work on another change project which in ING. And, yeah, what can I say? I I just love it. I
building something completely new from scratch, really improving something that existing, and having an impact is something that truly energizes me. And, when Wouter and I talked about our
experiences with change projects, we we that migrations always played a crucial role, whether you liked it or not, but it is what it is.
And that's why I'm especially proud of what we did in ING Germany in the last years, where we basically built a whole new business segment from scratch.
And that's the example I want to dive a bit deeper into. So, for the longest time, ING in Germany did not have a segment or a banking
offer for those small and medium-sized companies. So, the the freelancers, the family businesses, the startups, that was not there. And to get into that market fast, ING
bought the startup Lendico, a fintech startup offering loans for for companies. And we took that startup and integrated it into ING Germany. And that didn't only mean the product,
but this also meant the tech stack. And I mean, that was a startup, like they had to be fast as well. So, we also
integrated their shortcuts and and their technical depths that they had. And that was part of ING Germany now then as well. And that's when the real migration story
actually began. So, after integrating Lendico, we had loans. But I mean, companies have more needs than that. They need the whole banking portfolio. They need a savings account, they need a
current account. And that's why only 1 year later, we already built a savings account and launched it. And then again, only 1 year later, we
launched a current account. So, we were really going at crazy speed launching new products, and that is a huge challenge for our tech setup.
Because I mean, your architecture has to facilitate this, your tech stack has to, too. And there we faced a lot of challenges and this is when we realized that
migrations is not something that happens somewhere at the end of the road, but it is something that you really have to take into consideration in every step
of your project and in every phase your product goes to as you scale and as you mature. And to facilitate that growth and not
drown in our own shortcuts and tech debts that we did to facilitate this crazy growth, we came up with the tech migration model. And if you look at it, we have the
x-axis, this is the time, and the y-axis is the organizational value. So, the value a product has over the time for the organization. And we added an
additional layer to this, which is the migration mode in every phase. That model is inspired by um Lex Sisney's framework of organizational physics. And for those who don't know him, Lex
Sisney is a guy who focuses a lot on how organizations develop over time, especially on startups. And we took this idea of having basically every product we build as kind
of a mini startup. And to really look at the mode of migration we have to adjust in every step of that phase. So, the first one is the spotted phase.
There's not that much happening. Like, you're still exploring, so there is no migration. The next one is the piloted phase. There you build your first pilot and you
try to prevent early migrations. Next one is the built phase, where you actually then build your product. And this is also where you build for
migration. After that follows the scaled phase. You also can see that like the value for the organization for your product peaks there. And this is where you're forced
into refactoring in order to facilitate that growth of your product. And then we go down into the operated phase. There you have continuous upgrades to
keep your setup stable until the very end where you have the graceful shutdown where you have to kill your product. Because yeah, everything in tech ends
eventually. And now we want to walk you through those different phases on the example of building up our new segment business banking. >> So, we are in the sprout phase. This is
really where it starts. This is the place where you don't think about migrations at all. This is you have all the freedom of the world.
In our example, this is when we acquire the startup. We had to think about what Where are we going to build this new stack? Where are we going to build these
products? And there were a couple of options. You can expand on a startup that you have already gotten, but that means you you will maintain two
different stacks. Then we had the option, let's integrate it completely inside ING Germany, but it was also a stack that was also migrating. Or we had the option to go
for a global stack with a global offering of ING. After doing a couple of tryouts, we determined that the global offering of ING was the best way forward. It had a
lot of features available for us that we could use. We didn't have to think about authentication flows, customer data storage, analytical tools, web app
development. All of these things we build globally for all the countries where ING is working in. So, when we went for that approach, uh that meant that we didn't have to
think about any migrations. We could speed up incredibly fast and work on these new offerings without having to think about how is this all going to tie
together. What's really important in this phase is to reuse instead of recreate. >> And the next step is the piloted phase. So, there the product is increasing its
potential value for the organization, and this is where you focus on early migrations. So, for us this meant that we wanted to build something fast. Like the setup is still
in the storming and forming phase. Like everyone's running around trying to push for progress because you want to have something that you can show, something
that you can test. And this is really when we started with rapid prototyping. And the good part is everyone uses banking products. So, we
didn't have to wait for like a certain friends and family phase, but we showed our customer flows and we demoed them to our colleagues just very early on
because I mean everyone has a bit of an idea like how a good banking experience can look like. We use it daily. And the good part was that under our
colleagues we actually find some people who have side businesses. Like they had their own company already. And the cool part was that those people
would be our potential customers. So, we got feedback very very early on and we had only built very little to do so. And this meant that there was also
only very little to throw away because this is really the phase where you go for failing fast. You don't want to invent that much yet. You really want to
test it and see what works. And what we did is that at that time we were not quite sure yet what from our global stack we could reuse.
And we didn't want to wait for that either because we didn't have the time. And so, we already started building something that was not tied into our
legacy systems and was not focusing on global stack, but we just built something separately. And this really helped because then we didn't have to migrate away from a
flawed system at such an early stage where you really do not have the time or the capacity for this. And the next one is the build it phase.
We took all our learnings that we got from this piloted phase, all the feedback that we got from our colleagues and also from other test users and
started building the actual thing. And then we fell into a very common trap. And this is that we got super overwhelmed with all the requirements
for potential feature improvements like AI supported channels like sub-accounts for better overview, certain rights for your cards and uh all of this like backup options that
really go for every edge case. And the problem was that this continued. So while we were building, we had so much side noise coming in like a new
idea nearly every day or every week. And yeah, this comic really describes it pretty well what happened and I think that every one of you who works in
product development has probably faced that too. So while we went, we really had to make sure that we keep our scope under control. And in addition, the build it phase was
the phase where we went a bit away from this storming and forming into a more functional setup. Really people focused now on more on having one hat and
actually focusing on one thing and this structure already helped us to grow. And the biggest learning I would say that we had in this phase was the
management of technical debt. So this was now the time when we noticed that there are global features that we could reuse but they will not be ready on time.
It just didn't fit with the timeline that we had and we wanted to go to the market fast. And so we had to make the decision that
today we will build our own local stuff on our local stack in Germany knowing very damn well that we will have to migrate away from that to the global
stack once it's ready. So, yeah, that was additional effort being put in. And we had this further examples as well. Like there were some
fallback options and some stability topics that we said we will not need them now, but we know that we will have to pay that back later.
And this is really an important lesson. Like it's not about avoiding those tech debts, but it's about knowing that you take them, document them, and treat them
like a financial loan. So, you know, we bought speed today, but we know extremely well that this comes with an interest fee, and this comes with a deadline where you
have to pay it back. And you need to do this later than to scale. >> And now we get to the scaled phase. And the scaled phase is really the proof
of the pudding. You see the organizational value, it peaks. So, this is really where you have most of the value. All the preparations happened before are
for this scaled phase. This is also a phase that we are in right now. We built the features. The features are live. The customers are coming in, but more
customers can come in than you can handle at that point. The technical debt that was a conscious choice before is now starting to hit
that limit. Now you're going to find that the shortcuts that you took are now actually causing incidents. They're making you slower. You're not able to
release features as fast anymore uh as you were before. For us this really was an eye-opener within the release of the other different features. After we opened the
savings account, we wanted to go right away into creating new products. But the the first one was just life. And then the customers started coming in and
we saw actually incidents happening. We saw latency, we saw bugs appearing. So, we had to fix those at the same time and we couldn't do that. We had a forced
delay on our new product because we couldn't scale yet. So, we had to work on that first. So, we focused on that and then
afterwards we worked on the new product. I think a lot of you are familiar familiar with the relative cost of fixing bugs. If you have a bug and you detect it
early, then the relative cost of fixing it is very low. But, the further you go, the more impact it has. What a lot of people don't
realize is about the exponential growth of this interest that you're paying. With the technical debt that you have, it's the same. The later you get, it's
not like a loan or a mortgage that you have or you have just a five or 10% increase per year. When you don't fix it
early enough, the impact can be tenfold. You can bring down systems and if you don't migrate things at all, you can even crash your whole product.
And another thing that can happen is that it actually hits your morale. If you keep having issues with your production environment where you really want to
scale, then it's not only bad for the users, but you think like, why can we not keep working on these new products? Because we want to work keep working on
these new products. So, the challenging part about the scale it phase is really about balancing the change and the run. How much are you going to focus on
maintaining your systems versus how much are you going to focus on adding still the new features to compete with the market? It's very important also to not get
overwhelmed. You're going to get a lot of requests, and not just from your customers. You're going to get them from your management, from your stakeholders,
from everywhere around. And it's really important to keep your product stable in this phase. And then we get to the operated phase. The operated phase is the first time
where we actually see the organizational value going down. This is where we go more into a stable mode. We don't develop new features anymore. We
just have to maintain our product. You can also think of this phase as the phase where you actually constantly migrate, because the requests that are
coming in are not going to be built as new feature. It's uh move away from this repository, use this other dependency, use this other AI
tooling that we have developed inside the company. The challenging part here is how do you uh keep focusing on reserving this capacity for this change that is coming
in? Because we want to work on the latest part, like the operated phase does not It's not necessarily the most interesting phase. But we also want to here focus on
improving the efficiency, because if we keep doing the things the same way that we're doing before, eventually we're going to spend way too much time on
this. Time that we could have also spent on going towards the next product. In the operated phase, um you might notice coming from uh
XKCD uh about how reliant we are on certain technologies that we are not even aware about. In the operated phase, you also have these technologies. They're
somewhere there. If you don't know that they're there, and at some point they fall over because, you know, they shut down or there is a patch and it doesn't
work anymore, yeah, then you have another problem. So, even though the operated phase can seem like a not so interesting phase, it's still a very crucial phase to keep the
whole system running. >> And that brings us to the last stage, with which is the killer one. This is where the organizational value of that
product hits the zero. And the only thing you can do is a graceful shutdown. And that is the hardest stage because I mean as we build things
we get emotionally attached to it like whether we like it or not. And it feels a bit like building your own house. Of course it has its flaws
like maybe there is this one window that never really fully opens. There is the bathroom with already some cracks in the tile. But you built this together with
your team. And now you're the one who has to tear it down. And that is really hard but a graceful shutdown is also part of the life cycle
and that's how it is. We didn't have to do that with business banking yet. Um however, what we had to do is to shut
several features down already. And one example was that we noticed in our onboarding funnel so the onboarding people go through to get our products,
they got stuck on a page. And we thought okay like probably they don't understand what's going on or they struggle with the information that we
want and we came up with a feature there was a lot of pressure because of course we wanted to improve the customer experience there. We launched super
quickly. We made it on time. Everyone was super happy. And yeah, when we monitored the data in the next weeks, we noticed that even
more people now dropped out. So we really thought we did something there and we did. We made the customer experience worse. And there went a lot of emotion into
that feature but we noticed that it didn't really help with what we wanted and so the only thing that we could do is just shut it down immediately. We had
to roll back. We had to inform everyone super quick but because we acted so fast at least we could limit the customer impact that it had and this is what
counts in the end. And we communicated it early to the customers, to the stakeholders, finished it, and we retired it with intention. And yeah, that's not easy. But at the
same time, we could take those learnings and the capacity it freed up to to monitor it and to develop it further to actually work on something in the end
that does. And this is the end of the kill it phase. Cuz either you migrate to something completely new or you have to migrate to a newer
version, but it is definitely an end that creates a new beginning for you. >> So, some key takeaways of this presentation. You have to expect evolution. The change
is there whether you like it or not. You have to manage your technical debt. Treat it like a conscious choice. Treat it like a debt that you have to repay,
but with a very high interest. You have to adapt to the phase. If your application or your system goes through the life cycle, it's a different
way of thinking about migrations when you are in a different phase. So, maybe you want to procrastinate, maybe you want to postpone certain changes, or
maybe you want to do them now to not pay for them later. That depends on the circumstances. And kill it with courage. Don't get too
affected too attached to the product. Some things are not meant to live. Nothing is actually meant to live forever. Thank you for joining this presentation.
